With no real difference, the simulation shows the false winner rate jumping from about 5% to roughly a quarter of all tests.

Fixes used in practice: decide the sample size before you start and look once, or use a sequential test built for repeated looks. Either way, a significant result you went fishing for is weaker evidence than it looks.

Learn the idea: [Confidence intervals](https://monte.markets/learn/ci.md)

Next game: [The long run](https://monte.markets/play/long-run.md)

### S&P 500 simulator: the long run

Page: https://monte.markets/play/long-run/

98 years of real S&P 500 returns, played out 2,000 ways.

Game 8 of 10 in [Play](https://monte.markets/play/).

#### What’s going on

The **arithmetic mean** averages the yearly returns. The **geometric mean** is the rate your money actually compounded at: `(Π(1 + rₜ))^(1/n) − 1`. The geometric mean is always lower when returns move around, by roughly `σ² / 2`. For the S&P 500 since 1928 that gap is about 1.8 percentage points a year.

The simulation is a **bootstrap Monte Carlo**. Each future draws real historical years at random, with replacement. Repeat 2,000 times and read off the percentiles. It keeps every real crash and boom, but it assumes years are independent, so it ignores streaks and changing regimes. Treat it as a model, not a forecast.

Data: annual total returns from Aswath Damodaran’s *Historical Returns on Stocks, Bonds and Bills* at NYU Stern, updated January 5, 2026.

For learning, not investment advice.

Learn the idea: [How spread out is it](https://monte.markets/learn/spread.md)

Next game: [Price an option](https://monte.markets/play/options.md)

### Monte Carlo option pricing

Page: https://monte.markets/play/options/

Simulate stock paths and watch the price close in on Black-Scholes.

Game 9 of 10 in [Play](https://monte.markets/play/).

#### What’s going on

A **call** pays `max(S_T − K, 0)` at expiry; a **put** pays `max(K − S_T, 0)`. To price one, simulate the stock under **risk-neutral** rules: it grows at the interest rate, `S_T = S₀ · exp((r − σ²/2)T + σ√T · Z)` with Z a standard normal draw. Average the payoffs, discount by `e^(−rT)`, and you have a Monte Carlo price.

**Black-Scholes** does the same average in closed form: `C = S₀N(d₁) − Ke^(−rT)N(d₂)`, with `d₁ = [ln(S₀/K) + (r + σ²/2)T] / (σ√T)` and `d₂ = d₁ − σ√T`. N is the normal CDF from the normal curve topic. At S₀ = K = 100, one year, 5% and σ = 20%, the call is worth $10.45.

The Monte Carlo error shrinks like `1/√n`: four times the paths, half the error. That is why the shaded band narrows slowly, and why banks use Monte Carlo for options too complex for a formula.

A textbook model (constant volatility, no dividends). For learning, not investment advice.

Learn the idea: [The normal curve](https://monte.markets/learn/normal.md)

Next game: [Election night](https://monte.markets/play/election.md)

### Election night

Page: https://monte.markets/play/election/

Call the race from polls, then see why a 2-point lead is close to a coin flip.

Game 10 of 10 in [Play](https://monte.markets/play/).

#### What’s going on

A poll of *n* people estimates a share *p* with a **95% margin of error** of about `1.96 × √[p(1 − p)/n]`. Near a 50/50 race that is close to `1/√n`: about ±4.9 points for 400 people, ±3.1 for 1,000 and ±2.0 for 2,500. To halve the margin you need four times the people.

That headline margin is on each candidate’s share. The **lead**, A minus B, has about twice the margin, because a voter who switches adds to one side and takes from the other. A poll of 1,000 is good to about ±6 points on the lead, so a 2-point lead sits well inside the noise. With a true 2-point lead, one poll of 1,000 shows the wrong leader about 26% of the time.

**Averaging** polls works like one bigger poll. Five polls of 1,000 act like a single poll of 5,000, so the margin shrinks by √5 and the wrong leader rate falls to about 8%. Ten polls bring it near 2%.

Saying **how sure** you are is scored with the **Brier score**, `(outcome − p)²`, where outcome is 1 if A wins and 0 if not. It is a proper scoring rule: your best average comes from saying exactly what you believe. Shading a 70% hunch up to 95% costs you over many races. Chips are the same score moved so that 50% pays nothing: `100 × (1 − Brier) − 75`.

The formula only counts **sampling error**, the luck of who gets picked. Real polls also miss because of who answers, who actually turns out to vote and how questions are worded. Those errors tend to push every poll the same way, so averaging cannot cancel them. That is why real elections miss the polls by more than the margin of error says.

Learn the idea: [Confidence intervals](https://monte.markets/learn/ci.md)

Next game: [Guess the correlation](https://monte.markets/play/correlation.md)

## Solvers

### Probability tree diagram calculator

Page: https://monte.markets/solve/tree/

Branches, then an outcome. Leave branch 3 blank for two; a blank P(branch) fills in.

Solver 1 of 11.

#### Inputs, with the starting numbers

- Branch 1 name: Online
- P(branch 1): 0.6
- P(outcome | branch 1): 0.3
- Branch 2 name: In store
- P(branch 2): blank
- P(outcome | branch 2): 0.1
- Branch 3 name (optional): blank
- P(branch 3): blank
- P(outcome | branch 3): blank
- Outcome name: Return

#### Examples

- **Online vs store returns**: Branch 1 name: Online; P(branch 1): 0.6; P(outcome | branch 1): 0.3; Branch 2 name: In store; P(outcome | branch 2): 0.1; Outcome name: Return
- **Interns and offers**: Branch 1 name: Intern; P(branch 1): 0.4; P(outcome | branch 1): 0.7; Branch 2 name: Non-intern; P(outcome | branch 2): 0.25; Outcome name: Offer
- **Three suppliers**: Branch 1 name: Supplier A; P(branch 1): 0.5; P(outcome | branch 1): 0.02; Branch 2 name: Supplier B; P(branch 2): 0.3; P(outcome | branch 2): 0.03; Branch 3 name (optional): Supplier C; P(outcome | branch 3): 0.05; Outcome name: Defect
- **Medical test**: Branch 1 name: Sick; P(branch 1): 0.01; P(outcome | branch 1): 0.95; Branch 2 name: Healthy; P(outcome | branch 2): 0.05; Outcome name: Positive

#### Answers for the starting numbers

|   | Return | not Return | Total |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Online | 0.18 | 0.42 | 0.6 |
| In store | 0.04 | 0.36 | 0.4 |
| Total | 0.22 | 0.78 | 1 |

1. P(Return) = **0.22**
   - Work: 0.6 × 0.3 + 0.4 × 0.1 = 0.18 + 0.04. Add every Return branch (In store = 1 minus the others).
2. P(not Return) = **0.78**
   - Work: 1 − 0.22
3. P(Return | Online) = **0.3**
   - Work: Given.
4. P(Return | In store) = **0.1**
   - Work: Given.
5. P(Online and Return) = **0.18**
   - Work: And means multiply along the branch: 0.6 × 0.3
6. P(Online | Return) = **0.8182**
   - Work: Bayes: 0.18 ÷ 0.22. The given (Return) is the new total.
7. P(In store | Return) = **0.1818**
   - Work: Bayes: 0.04 ÷ 0.22
8. P(Online | not Return) = **0.5385**
   - Work: 0.42 ÷ 0.78
9. P(In store | not Return) = **0.4615**
   - Work: 0.36 ÷ 0.78
10. P(Online or Return) = **0.64**
    - Work: 0.6 + 0.22 − 0.18. Or means add, minus the overlap.
11. Are Online and Return independent? = **No**
    - Work: P(Online and Return) = 0.18 is not P(Online) × P(Return) = 0.132.
12. Trap: is P(Online | Return) the same as P(Return | Online)? = **No: 0.8182 vs 0.3**
    - Work: Flipping the given changes the denominator.
13. Most likely single outcome = **Online and not Return**
    - Work: 0.42, the biggest branch.
14. Two independent times: Return both = **0.0484**
    - Work: 0.22²
15. Two independent times: at least one Return = **0.3916**
    - Work: 1 − 0.78²

### Draws with and without replacement

Page: https://monte.markets/solve/draws/

Two draws, with or without putting the first back.

Solver 2 of 11.

#### Inputs, with the starting numbers

- Count of kind 1: 4
- Count of kind 2: 8
- Kind 1 name: Green
- Kind 2 name: White
- Replacement: Without (default)
  - Choices: Without (default); With

#### Examples

- **4 green, 8 white**: Count of kind 1: 4; Count of kind 2: 8; Kind 1 name: Green; Kind 2 name: White; Replacement: Without (default)
- **Parts: 3 bad of 20**: Count of kind 1: 3; Count of kind 2: 17; Kind 1 name: Defective; Kind 2 name: Good; Replacement: Without (default)
- **Aces in a deck**: Count of kind 1: 4; Count of kind 2: 48; Kind 1 name: Ace; Kind 2 name: Other; Replacement: Without (default)

#### Answers for the starting numbers

| First, then second | Work | Probability |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Green, Green | 4/12 × 3/11 | 0.0909 |
| Green, White | 4/12 × 8/11 | 0.2424 |
| White, Green | 8/12 × 4/11 | 0.2424 |
| White, White | 8/12 × 7/11 | 0.4242 |
| Total |   | 1 |

1. P(Green first) = **1/3 = 0.3333**
   - Work: 4 of 12
2. P(Green then Green) = **1/11 = 0.0909**
   - Work: 4/12 × 3/11. One Green is gone, so both counts drop by 1.
3. P(Green then White) = **8/33 = 0.2424**
   - Work: 4/12 × 8/11
4. P(White then Green) = **8/33 = 0.2424**
   - Work: 8/12 × 4/11
5. P(White then White) = **14/33 = 0.4242**
   - Work: 8/12 × 7/11
6. One of each, either order = **16/33 = 0.4848**
   - Work: Both orders: 8/33 + 8/33.
7. At least one Green = **19/33 = 0.5758**
   - Work: 1 − P(White, White)
8. At least one White = **10/11 = 0.9091**
   - Work: 1 − P(Green, Green)
9. P(White second | Green first) = **8/11 = 0.7273**
   - Work: Given, so shrink the box: 8 White left of 11.
10. P(Green second | Green first) = **3/11 = 0.2727**
    - Work: 3 left of 11
11. P(Green on second), first unknown = **1/3 = 0.3333**
    - Work: Same as the first draw. Trap question.
12. P(Green first | Green second) = **0.2727**
    - Work: Bayes: P(Green,Green) ÷ P(Green second) = 0.0909 ÷ 0.3333
13. Are the draws independent? = **No**
    - Work: P(Green second | Green first) = 0.2727, not 0.3333. Without replacement, the first draw changes the box.

### Conditional probability calculator

Page: https://monte.markets/solve/events/

Give P(A), P(B) and P(A and B).

Solver 3 of 11.

#### Inputs, with the starting numbers

- P(A): 0.6
- P(B): 0.5
- P(A and B): 0.3

#### Examples

- **Die: 6 given over 3**: P(A): 1/6; P(B): 1/2; P(A and B): 1/6
- **Independent**: P(A): 0.6; P(B): 0.5; P(A and B): 0.3
- **Mutually exclusive**: P(A): 0.25; P(B): 0.45; P(A and B): 0

#### Answers for the starting numbers

|   | B | not B | Total |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A | 0.3 | 0.3 | 0.6 |
| not A | 0.2 | 0.2 | 0.4 |
| Total | 0.5 | 0.5 | 1 |

1. P(A or B) = **0.8**
   - Work: 0.6 + 0.5 − 0.3. Subtract the overlap once.
2. P(A | B) = **0.6**
   - Work: 0.3 ÷ 0.5. B is the new total.
3. P(B | A) = **0.5**
   - Work: 0.3 ÷ 0.6
4. P(not A) = **0.4**
   - Work: 1 − 0.6
5. P(neither) = **0.2**
   - Work: 1 − P(A or B)
6. P(A only) = **0.3**
   - Work: 0.6 − 0.3
7. P(exactly one) = **0.5**
   - Work: P(A or B) − P(A and B)
8. Independent? = **Yes**
   - Work: P(A) × P(B) = 0.3 equals P(A and B) = 0.3.
9. Mutually exclusive? = **No**
   - Work: They overlap, P(A and B) = 0.3.

### Binomial probability calculator

Page: https://monte.markets/solve/trials/

Same chance each try: none, at least one, exactly k.

Solver 4 of 11.

#### Inputs, with the starting numbers

- P(success) each time: 0.7
- Number of trials n: 5
- Exactly k: 4

#### Examples

- **Free throws: 70%, 5 shots**: P(success) each time: 0.7; Number of trials n: 5; Exactly k: 4
- **Coin: 3 flips**: P(success) each time: 0.5; Number of trials n: 3; Exactly k: 2
- **Die: a six in 4 rolls**: P(success) each time: 1/6; Number of trials n: 4; Exactly k: 1

#### Answers for the starting numbers

| Successes | Probability |
| --- | --- |
| 0 | 0.0024 |
| 1 | 0.0284 |
| 2 | 0.1323 |
| 3 | 0.3087 |
| 4 | 0.3601 |
| 5 | 0.1681 |

1. P(none) = **0.0024**
   - Work: 0.3^5. And means multiply.
2. P(at least one) = **0.9976**
   - Work: 1 − 0.3^5. Always use the complement.
3. P(all 5) = **0.1681**
   - Work: 0.7^5
4. P(exactly 4) = **0.3601**
   - Work: 5 × 0.7^4 × 0.3^1. The first number counts the orders.
5. P(at most 4) = **0.8319**
   - Work: Add exactly 0 through 4
6. P(at least 4) = **0.5282**
   - Work: 1 − P(at most 3)
7. P(exactly 4 | at least one) = **0.361**
   - Work: 0.3601 ÷ 0.9976. Given at least one, so that is the new total.
8. Expected number np = **3.5**
   - Work: 5 × 0.7
9. SD √(npq) = **1.0247**
   - Work: √(5 × 0.7 × 0.3)

### Poisson distribution calculator

Page: https://monte.markets/solve/poisson/

A rate per unit. Scale it to the window first.

Solver 5 of 11.

#### Inputs, with the starting numbers

- Rate per unit: 4
- Unit name: hour
- Window, in units: 1
- Count k: 3

#### Examples

- **Calls: 4 an hour, exactly 3**: Rate per unit: 4; Unit name: hour; Window, in units: 1; Count k: 3
- **Calls: 1 or fewer in 30 minutes**: Rate per unit: 4; Unit name: hour; Window, in units: 0.5; Count k: 1
- **Typos: 1.5 a page, 2 pages**: Rate per unit: 1.5; Unit name: page; Window, in units: 2; Count k: 2

#### Answers for the starting numbers

| Count | P(exactly) | P(this many or fewer) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | 0.0183 | 0.0183 |
| 1 | 0.0733 | 0.0916 |
| 2 | 0.1465 | 0.2381 |
| 3 | 0.1954 | 0.4335 |
| 4 | 0.1954 | 0.6288 |
| 5 | 0.1563 | 0.7851 |
| 6 | 0.1042 | 0.8893 |
| 7 | 0.0595 | 0.9489 |
| 8 | 0.0298 | 0.9786 |
| 9 | 0.0132 | 0.9919 |
| 10 | 0.0053 | 0.9972 |

1. λ for this window = **4**
   - Work: 4 per hour × 1 hour. Scale the rate first; this is the step people miss.
2. P(exactly 3) = **0.1954**
   - Work: e^−4 × 4^3 / 3!
3. P(3 or fewer) = **0.4335**
   - Work: Add P(0) through P(3)
4. P(fewer than 3) = **0.2381**
   - Work: Add P(0) through P(2)
5. P(at least 3) = **0.7619**
   - Work: 1 − P(2 or fewer)
6. P(more than 3) = **0.5665**
   - Work: 1 − P(3 or fewer)
7. P(none) = **0.0183**
   - Work: e^−4
8. P(at least one) = **0.9817**
   - Work: 1 − e^−4
9. P(exactly 3 | at least one) = **0.199**
   - Work: P(3) / P(at least one) = 0.1954 / 0.9817. Given at least one, divide by that.
10. Mean and variance = **4**
    - Work: Both equal λ for a Poisson. SD = √λ = 2

### Normal distribution calculator

Page: https://monte.markets/solve/normal/

Mean and SD, then any value or cutoff.

Solver 6 of 11.

#### Inputs, with the starting numbers

- Mean μ: 500
- SD σ: 40
- Value x: 540
- Second value (for between): blank
- Top or bottom %: 5
- How many in a row (all below x): 3
- Sample size n (for the average): 16

#### Examples

- **Battery: over 540 hours**: Mean μ: 500; SD σ: 40; Value x: 540; Top or bottom %: 5; How many in a row (all below x): 1; Sample size n (for the average): 1
- **Between 450 and 560**: Mean μ: 500; SD σ: 40; Value x: 450; Second value (for between): 560; Top or bottom %: 5; How many in a row (all below x): 1; Sample size n (for the average): 1
- **Three all under 480**: Mean μ: 500; SD σ: 40; Value x: 480; Top or bottom %: 5; How many in a row (all below x): 3; Sample size n (for the average): 1
- **Average of 16 under 510**: Mean μ: 500; SD σ: 40; Value x: 510; Top or bottom %: 5; How many in a row (all below x): 1; Sample size n (for the average): 16

#### Answers for the starting numbers

1. z for x = 540 = **1**
   - Work: (x − μ) / σ = (540 − 500) / 40. How many SDs from the mean.
2. P(X < 540) = **0.8413**
   - Work: Φ(1)
3. P(X > 540) = **0.1587**
   - Work: 1 − Φ(1)
4. Top 5% starts at = **565.7941**
   - Work: μ + zσ with z = 1.645: 500 + 1.645 × 40. Area first, then z, then x.
5. Bottom 5% ends at = **434.2059**
   - Work: 500 − 1.645 × 40
6. All 3 below 540 = **0.5956**
   - Work: 0.8413^3. Independent, so multiply.
7. All 3 above 540 = **0.004**
   - Work: 0.1587^3
8. At least one of 3 above 540 = **0.4044**
   - Work: 1 − 0.8413^3
9. Standard error of the average = **10**
   - Work: σ / √n = 40 / √16. Averages wobble less than single values.
10. z for an average of 540 = **4**
    - Work: (540 − 500) / 10
11. P(average of 16 < 540) = **> 0.9999**
    - Work: Φ(4)
12. P(average of 16 > 540) = **< 0.0001**
    - Work: 1 − Φ(4)
13. Empirical rule check = **68% within 460 to 540; 95% within 420 to 580; 99.7% within 380 to 620**
    - Work: μ ± 1, 2 and 3 SD.

### Sampling distribution calculator

Page: https://monte.markets/solve/samp/

Every sample of size n from a small population.

Solver 7 of 11.

#### Inputs, with the starting numbers

- Population values, separated by commas: 1, 2, 3, 6
- Sample size n: 2
- Drawing: With replacement
  - Choices: With replacement; Without replacement
- Cutoff c, for P(x̄ ≤ c): 2

#### Examples

- **Four values, n = 2**: Population values, separated by commas: 1, 2, 3, 6; Sample size n: 2; Drawing: With replacement; Cutoff c, for P(x̄ ≤ c): 2
- **Five prices, 3 different ones**: Population values, separated by commas: 4, 5, 7, 9, 10; Sample size n: 3; Drawing: Without replacement; Cutoff c, for P(x̄ ≤ c): 6
- **Two dice, average roll**: Population values, separated by commas: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6; Sample size n: 2; Drawing: With replacement; Cutoff c, for P(x̄ ≤ c): 2.5

#### Answers for the starting numbers

| x̄ | Samples | P(x̄) | P(x̄ or less) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 1 | 0.0625 | 0.0625 |
| 1.5 | 2 | 0.125 | 0.1875 |
| 2 | 3 | 0.1875 | 0.375 |
| 2.5 | 2 | 0.125 | 0.5 |
| 3 | 1 | 0.0625 | 0.5625 |
| 3.5 | 2 | 0.125 | 0.6875 |
| 4 | 2 | 0.125 | 0.8125 |
| 4.5 | 2 | 0.125 | 0.9375 |
| 6 | 1 | 0.0625 | 1 |

1. Population mean μ = **3**
   - Work: Σx / N = 12 / 4
2. Population SD σ = **1.8708**
   - Work: Divide by N = 4 because this is the whole population. σ² = 3.5.
3. Possible samples = **16**
   - Work: N^n = 4^2. Order counts and repeats are allowed, so every one is equally likely.
4. Average of all the sample means = **3**
   - Work: It equals μ: x̄ is an unbiased estimator.
5. Standard error of x̄ = **1.3229**
   - Work: σ / √n = 1.8708 / √2. Same as the SD of the list of means.
6. P(x̄ ≤ 2), exact = **0.375**
   - Work: 6 of the 16 samples have a mean of 2 or less.
7. Normal approximation = **0.2248**
   - Work: z = (2 − 3) / 1.3229 = -0.7559. Rough at a small n; the exact count above is the answer.

### Confidence interval and sample size calculator

Page: https://monte.markets/solve/ci/

A mean or a proportion, then the sample size.

Solver 8 of 11.

#### Inputs, with the starting numbers

- Type: Mean, s from the sample (t)
  - Choices: Mean, s from the sample (t); Mean, σ known (z); Proportion
- Confidence: 95%
  - Choices: 90%; 95%; 99%
- Sample size n: 25
- Mean x̄: 42.5
  - Shown when Type is Mean, s from the sample (t) or Mean, σ known (z)
- SD s or σ: 6.2
  - Shown when Type is Mean, s from the sample (t) or Mean, σ known (z)
- Count with the trait: blank
  - Shown when Type is Proportion
- Target E (for sample size): 2
- E is: The margin (±)
  - Choices: The margin (±); The full length

#### Examples

- **Delivery times: 95%, n 25**: Type: Mean, s from the sample (t); Confidence: 95%; Sample size n: 25; Mean x̄: 42.5; SD s or σ: 6.2; Target E (for sample size): 2; E is: The margin (±)
- **Survey: 240 of 400 say yes**: Type: Proportion; Confidence: 95%; Sample size n: 400; Count with the trait: 240; Target E (for sample size): 0.06; E is: The full length

#### Answers for the starting numbers

1. Critical value = **t = 2.064**
   - Work: t with n − 1 = 24 df, 95% two-sided. σ unknown, so t.
2. Standard error = **1.24**
   - Work: s / √n = 6.2 / √25
3. 95% interval for μ = **39.9406 to 45.0594**
   - Work: x̄ ± 2.064 × 1.24 = 42.5 ± 2.5594
4. Margin of error = **2.5594**
   - Work: 2.064 × 1.24
5. Sample size for ± 2 (z) = **37**
   - Work: (zσ/E)² = (1.96 × 6.2 / 2)² = 36.9178. Round up. The usual textbook answer.
6. Same, if you keep t = 2.064 = **41**
   - Work: (2.064 × 6.2 / 2)² = 40.9395. Check which one your book or teacher uses.

### Hypothesis test calculator

Page: https://monte.markets/solve/test/

z, t or proportion. The p-value and the decision.

Solver 9 of 11.

#### Inputs, with the starting numbers

- Test: Mean, σ known (z)
  - Choices: Mean, σ known (z); Mean, s from the sample (t); Proportion (z)
- H₁: Not equal (two-sided)
  - Choices: Not equal (two-sided); Less than (left tail); Greater than (right tail)
- H₀ value, μ₀ or p₀: 250
- Sample size n: 36
- Sample mean x̄: 247.5
  - Shown when Test is Mean, σ known (z) or Mean, s from the sample (t)
- σ or s: 6
  - Shown when Test is Mean, σ known (z) or Mean, s from the sample (t)
- Count with the trait: blank
  - Shown when Test is Proportion (z)
- α: 0.05
  - Choices: 0.10; 0.05; 0.01

#### Examples

- **Machine: 247.5 against 250**: Test: Mean, σ known (z); H₁: Not equal (two-sided); H₀ value, μ₀ or p₀: 250; Sample size n: 36; Sample mean x̄: 247.5; σ or s: 6; α: 0.05
- **Bags under 500 g? (t)**: Test: Mean, s from the sample (t); H₁: Less than (left tail); H₀ value, μ₀ or p₀: 500; Sample size n: 16; Sample mean x̄: 492; σ or s: 12; α: 0.05
- **230 of 400 prefer A**: Test: Proportion (z); H₁: Not equal (two-sided); H₀ value, μ₀ or p₀: 0.5; Sample size n: 400; Count with the trait: 230; α: 0.05

#### Answers for the starting numbers

1. Hypotheses = **H₀: μ = 250 H₁: μ ≠ 250**
   - Work: H₀ holds the equals sign. H₁ is the claim you want evidence for.
2. Standard error = **1**
   - Work: σ / √n = 6 / √36
3. Test statistic z = **-2.5**
   - Work: (x̄ − 250) / 1
4. Critical value = **z = ±1.960**
   - Work: Two-sided: α/2 = 0.025 in each tail. Reject if the statistic is past it.
5. p-value = **0.0124**
   - Work: 2 × P(z > |-2.5|)
6. Decision = **Reject H₀**
   - Work: p-value 0.0124 < α = 0.05
7. In words = **The data are strong evidence that μ ≠ 250.**
   - Work: Say it about the population, at α = 0.05.
8. 95% interval for μ = **245.54 to 249.46**
   - Work: Leaves out 250, which matches the decision. A two-sided test and its interval always agree.

### Birthday problem calculator

Page: https://monte.markets/solve/bday/

Chance two people in a room share a birthday.

Solver 10 of 11.

#### Inputs, with the starting numbers

- People in the room: 40
- Days in a year: 365

#### Examples

- **A room of 40**: People in the room: 40; Days in a year: 365
- **22 people**: People in the room: 22; Days in a year: 365
- **23 people**: People in the room: 23; Days in a year: 365

#### Answers for the starting numbers

| People | P(shared birthday) |
| --- | --- |
| 2 | 0.0027 |
| 10 | 0.1169 |
| 20 | 0.4114 |
| 22 | 0.4757 |
| 23 | 0.5073 |
| 30 | 0.7063 |
| 40 (yours) | 0.8912 |
| 50 | 0.9704 |
| 57 | 0.9901 |

1. P(at least two share a birthday), n = 40 = **0.8912**
   - Work: 1 − P(all different). Complement, the same move as at least one.
2. P(all different birthdays) = **0.1088**
   - Work: 365/365 × 364/365 × 363/365 × ... × 326/365 (40 fractions)
3. P(someone shares YOUR birthday) = **0.1015**
   - Work: 1 − (364/365)^39. Different question: only pairs that include you count.
4. Number of pairs = **780**
   - Work: 40 × 39 / 2. Why it climbs so fast: every pair is a chance to match.
5. Expected matching pairs = **2.137**
   - Work: 780 / 365
6. People needed for a 50% chance = **23**
   - Work: The famous answer: 23 people
7. People needed for a 99% chance = **57**

### Descriptive statistics calculator

Page: https://monte.markets/solve/data/

Paste a list. Every summary, step by step.

Solver 11 of 11.

#### Inputs, with the starting numbers

- Numbers, separated by commas or spaces: 32, 25, 41, 25, 38, 29, 44, 25, 36

#### Examples

- **Commute minutes**: Numbers, separated by commas or spaces: 32, 25, 41, 25, 38, 29, 44, 25, 36
- **Weekly sales**: Numbers, separated by commas or spaces: 12, 18, 9, 15, 18, 21, 14

#### Answers for the starting numbers

1. Sorted (n = 9) = **25, 25, 25, 29, 32, 36, 38, 41, 44**
   - Work: Sort first. Median and mode fall out.
2. Mean x̄ = **32.7778**
   - Work: Σx / n = 295 / 9
3. Median = **32**
   - Work: Middle value, position 5
4. Mode = **25**
   - Work: Shows up 3 times.
5. Range = **19**
   - Work: 44 − 25
6. Deviations from x̄ = **-0.7778, -7.7778, 8.2222, -7.7778, 5.2222, -3.7778, 11.2222, -7.7778, 3.2222**
   - Work: They add to 0, which checks the mean.
7. Squared deviations, Σ = **427.5556**
   - Work: 0.6049 + 60.4938 + 67.6049 + 60.4938 + 27.2716 + 14.2716 + 125.9383 + 60.4938 + 10.3827
8. Sample variance s² = **53.4444**
   - Work: 427.5556 / 8. Sample, so divide by n − 1.
9. Sample SD s = **7.3106**
   - Work: √53.4444
10. Shortcut check = **53.4444**
    - Work: [Σx² − (Σx)²/n] / (n − 1) = (10,097 − 9669.4444) / 8
11. If the question says population = **47.5062 and σ = 6.8925**
    - Work: Divide by n = 9 instead.
12. Mean vs median = **Mean above median: maybe a right tail**
    - Work: The mean chases a tail; the median does not move. A hint about shape, not proof: plot it to be sure.

## Glossary

- Population (https://monte.markets/learn/data/): Every unit you care about. Example: Every customer of a bank, surveyed or not.
- Sample (https://monte.markets/learn/data/): The slice of the population you actually measure. Example: 500 customers picked at random.
- Parameter (https://monte.markets/learn/data/): A number that describes the population. Usually unknown. Example: The true average balance μ of all customers.
- Statistic (https://monte.markets/learn/data/): A number computed from a sample. It changes from sample to sample. Example: x̄, the average balance of your 500.
- Simple random sample (https://monte.markets/learn/data/): Every possible sample of size n has the same chance of being picked. Example: 50 names drawn from a hat holding every name.
- Stratified sample (https://monte.markets/learn/data/): Split the population into groups, then sample at random inside each. Example: 20 customers from each region, so every region shows up.
- Qualitative variable (https://monte.markets/learn/data/): Labels or categories, even if they come in an order. Example: Shirt size S, M, L.
- Quantitative variable (https://monte.markets/learn/data/): Numbers you can do arithmetic on. Example: Monthly sales in dollars.
- Discrete vs continuous (https://monte.markets/learn/data/): Discrete values are counted; continuous ones are measured and can fall anywhere. Example: Number of children vs height.
- Levels of measurement (https://monte.markets/learn/data/): Nominal (names), ordinal (order), interval (equal steps, no true zero), ratio (true zero). Example: Temperature in °C is interval; income is ratio.
- Mean (https://monte.markets/learn/center/): The balance point: add everything up and divide by how many. Example: 2, 4, 9: mean 5.
- Median (https://monte.markets/learn/center/): The middle value once sorted. Outliers barely move it. Example: 2, 4, 90: median 4, mean 32.
- Mode (https://monte.markets/learn/center/): The most common value. Example: Shoe sizes 8, 9, 9, 10: mode 9.
- Skew (https://monte.markets/learn/center/): A long tail on one side. The mean gets pulled toward the tail. Example: Incomes skew right, so mean > median.
- Outlier (https://monte.markets/learn/center/): A value far from the rest. Example: One $5M house on a street of $400k homes.
- Range (https://monte.markets/learn/spread/): Largest minus smallest. Example: 3 to 11: range 8.
- Variance (https://monte.markets/learn/spread/): The average squared distance from the mean (divide by n − 1 for a sample). Example: Units are squared, so we take the root.
- Standard deviation (https://monte.markets/learn/spread/): The typical distance from the mean, in the data's own units. Example: Returns average 8% with SD 6%.
- Coefficient of variation (https://monte.markets/learn/spread/): SD divided by the mean: risk per unit of reward. Example: SD 6 on mean 8 is CV 75%.
- z score (https://monte.markets/learn/spread/): How many SDs a value sits from the mean. Example: z = 2 means two SDs above average.
- Empirical rule (https://monte.markets/learn/spread/): For bell-shaped data, about 68%, 95% and 99.7% fall within 1, 2 and 3 SDs. Example: Mean 100, SD 15: 95% between 70 and 130.
- Interquartile range (https://monte.markets/learn/spread/): Q3 minus Q1, the spread of the middle half. Example: Ignores the extremes on both ends.
- Sample space (https://monte.markets/learn/prob/): Every possible outcome. Example: A die: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6.
- Event (https://monte.markets/learn/prob/): A set of outcomes you care about. Example: Rolling an even number.
- Complement (https://monte.markets/learn/prob/): Everything that is not the event. P(not A) = 1 − P(A). Example: P(at least one) = 1 − P(none).
- Mutually exclusive (https://monte.markets/learn/prob/): Two events that cannot happen together. Example: Rolling a 2 and a 5 on one roll.
- Independent (https://monte.markets/learn/prob/): Knowing one happened does not change the chance of the other. Example: Two separate coin flips.
- Conditional probability (https://monte.markets/learn/prob/): The chance of A once you know B happened: P(A and B) / P(B). Example: P(bag arrives | flight on time).
- Bayes' rule (https://monte.markets/learn/prob/): Flip a conditional around: from P(B | A) to P(A | B). Example: From test accuracy to the chance you really have it.
- Random variable (https://monte.markets/learn/rv/): A number whose value depends on chance. Example: Profit next month.
- Expected value (https://monte.markets/learn/rv/): The probability-weighted average: the long-run average over many repeats. Example: A die averages 3.5, though you never roll 3.5.
- Probability distribution (https://monte.markets/learn/rv/): A list or curve of every value and its probability. Example: Visits 0, 1, 2 with chances 0.5, 0.3, 0.2.
- Covariance (https://monte.markets/learn/two/): Whether two variables move together, in their combined units. Example: Positive when both rise together.
- Correlation (https://monte.markets/learn/two/): Covariance rescaled to sit between −1 and 1. Example: r = 0.8: a strong upward pattern.
- Diversification (https://monte.markets/learn/two/): Mixing assets that don't move together lowers total risk. Example: Low correlation means a lower portfolio SD.
- Factorial (https://monte.markets/learn/count/): n! = n × (n − 1) × … × 1: ways to order n things. Example: 4! = 24.
- Combination (https://monte.markets/learn/count/): Ways to choose k from n when order does not matter. Example: C(5, 2) = 10 pairs.
- Permutation (https://monte.markets/learn/count/): Ways to choose k from n when order matters. Example: P(5, 2) = 20 ordered pairs.
- Binomial distribution (https://monte.markets/learn/count/): Count of successes in n independent tries with the same chance p. Example: Heads in 10 flips.
- Hypergeometric distribution (https://monte.markets/learn/count/): Successes when you draw without replacement from a small group. Example: Defective parts in 4 picked from a box of 10.
- Poisson distribution (https://monte.markets/learn/poisson/): Events in a fixed window when they arrive at a steady rate λ. Example: Calls per hour at a help desk.
- Rate λ (https://monte.markets/learn/poisson/): The average count per window. Mean and variance both equal λ. Example: 3 per hour is λ = 6 over 2 hours.
- Normal distribution (https://monte.markets/learn/normal/): The bell curve, set by its mean and SD. Example: Heights, measurement errors, many averages.
- Standard normal (https://monte.markets/learn/normal/): The normal with mean 0 and SD 1. Every z table uses it. Example: Z ~ N(0, 1).
- Percentile (https://monte.markets/learn/normal/): The value with a given share of the data below it. Example: The 90th percentile has 90% below it.
- Uniform distribution (https://monte.markets/learn/normal/): Every value in a range is equally likely. Example: A wait between 0 and 20 minutes.
- Sampling distribution (https://monte.markets/learn/clt/): The distribution of a statistic over every possible sample. Example: All the x̄'s you could get with n = 36.
- Standard error (https://monte.markets/learn/clt/): The SD of a statistic: how much it wobbles from sample to sample. Example: σ / √n for a sample mean.
- Central Limit Theorem (https://monte.markets/learn/clt/): Averages of large samples are close to normal, whatever the population looks like. Example: Skewed incomes, but averages of 50 form a bell.
- Unbiased estimator (https://monte.markets/learn/clt/): A statistic whose average over all samples equals the parameter. Example: x̄ for μ, and s² with n − 1 for σ².
- Efficient estimator (https://monte.markets/learn/clt/): The unbiased estimator with the smallest spread. Example: For normal data, x̄ beats the median for estimating μ.
- Point estimate (https://monte.markets/learn/ci/): A single best guess for a parameter. Example: x̄ = 42.5.
- Confidence interval (https://monte.markets/learn/ci/): Estimate plus or minus a margin. Built this way, 95% catch the truth. Example: 42.5 ± 2.6.
- Margin of error (https://monte.markets/learn/ci/): The plus-or-minus part of an interval. Example: ± 3 points in a poll.
- Confidence level (https://monte.markets/learn/ci/): How often the method catches the truth in the long run. Example: 95%: about 95 of 100 intervals.
- t distribution (https://monte.markets/learn/ci/): Like the normal, with fatter tails. Used when σ is unknown and you use s. Example: t with 15 df for n = 16.
- Degrees of freedom (https://monte.markets/learn/ci/): How many values are free to vary. For one sample, n − 1. Example: n = 20 gives 19 df.
- Null hypothesis H₀ (https://monte.markets/learn/test/): The boring claim of no effect or no change. It holds the equals sign. Example: μ = 250 ml.
- Alternative hypothesis H₁ (https://monte.markets/learn/test/): What you want evidence for. Example: μ ≠ 250, or μ < 250.
- Test statistic (https://monte.markets/learn/test/): How many standard errors the sample landed from H₀. Example: z = −2.5.
- p-value (https://monte.markets/learn/test/): The chance of data at least this extreme if H₀ were true. Example: p = 0.012: rare under H₀.
- Significance level α (https://monte.markets/learn/test/): The cutoff for rejecting H₀, and the chance of a false alarm. Example: α = 0.05.
- Type I error (https://monte.markets/learn/test/): Rejecting a true H₀: a false alarm. Example: Calling a fair machine broken.
- Type II error (https://monte.markets/learn/test/): Keeping a false H₀: a missed signal. Example: Missing that the machine pours short.
- Power (https://monte.markets/learn/test/): The chance of catching a real effect: 1 − β. Example: Bigger samples have more power.
- One-sided vs two-sided (https://monte.markets/learn/test/): One-sided looks in one direction; two-sided looks for any difference. Example: H₁: μ < 500 vs H₁: μ ≠ 500.
- Regression line (https://monte.markets/learn/reg/): The straight line that best predicts y from x by least squares. Example: ŷ = 2 + 0.5x.
- Slope (https://monte.markets/learn/reg/): How much predicted y changes when x rises by 1. Example: 0.5 more sales per ad dollar.
- Intercept (https://monte.markets/learn/reg/): Predicted y when x is 0. Sometimes meaningless. Example: Sales with zero advertising.
- Residual (https://monte.markets/learn/reg/): Actual minus predicted: what the line missed. Example: Actual 10, predicted 8: residual 2.
- Least squares (https://monte.markets/learn/reg/): Pick the line with the smallest sum of squared residuals. Example: SSE is minimized.
- R² (https://monte.markets/learn/reg/): The share of the variation in y that the model explains. Example: R² = 0.81: 81% explained.
- Extrapolation (https://monte.markets/learn/reg/): Predicting outside the range of x you observed. Risky. Example: Ad spend of 50 when the data stop at 12.
- Multiple regression (https://monte.markets/learn/mreg/): Predicting y from several x's at once. Example: Price from size, age and location.
- Adjusted R² (https://monte.markets/learn/mreg/): R² with a penalty for adding predictors that do not help. Example: Falls when you add a useless variable.
- Dummy variable (https://monte.markets/learn/mreg/): A 0/1 column for a category. Use k − 1 of them for k categories. Example: North = 1, else 0.
- Multicollinearity (https://monte.markets/learn/mreg/): Predictors that move together, which makes slopes unstable. Example: VIF above 5 or 10 is a warning.
- F test (https://monte.markets/learn/mreg/): Tests whether the model as a whole explains anything. Example: F = MSR / MSE.
